In nineteen seventy-six, at the Judgment of Paris, America produced a French-style wine, better than the French.
Nine French judges sat and drank Cabernet Sauvignon, held up the unmarked bottle, and called it the best in the world.
The winning red came from the Stags Leap District in Napa, and the story was so famous, the bottle ended up in the Smithsonian.
After that, Napa wasn't farm country any more. It was the most famous red wine name in America.
Napa as a region is really small. The whole valley is a fraction of the size of Bordeaux, and that means prime vineyard land goes for half a million dollars an acre.
Most of the county is protected from development, so it can't get any bigger. So Napa producers can afford to charge hundreds per bottle.
Raptor and Crimson is made by Kevin Morrissey, who grew market standard wines at Etude and Ehlers Estate.
He pulls Cabernet from Stags Leap District, Oakville, Atlas Peak and Diamond Mountain, where the best vines are found.
He mixes this with more recent vines, to give some freshness to the blend, then ages it for eighteen months in American oak. And the result is stunning.
You get this potent hit of blackcurrant, plum and espresso to start, before the taste mellows on the palate, fading to subtle dark chocolate and tobacco notes that sit long on the tongue.
And it shows. The Tasting Panel gave it ninety-six points, and Vivino drinkers put it in the top four percent of wines in the world.
